final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

report.markdown:
# Training Plan: 14-Month Rescue Border Collie Mix (Pulling + Barks at Every Dog on Walks)

## 1. Hire a trainer, or DIY?

**Recommendation: Hybrid.** DIY the leash-pulling mechanics yourself (see plan below); budget for a short, targeted engagement with a professional trainer for the dog-reactivity/barking piece specifically.

Why:
- **Pulling** is a pure mechanics/reward-timing problem — very DIY-able with a standard loose-leash protocol. No professional needed for this alone.
- **Barking at every dog** is classic leash reactivity. This is one of the most common issues in the breed — border collies are highly visually alert and prone to over-arousal or frustration around other dogs on leash — and it typically responds well to gradual desensitization and counter-conditioning done at a safe distance, only closing that distance as the dog stays calm. Nothing here suggests aggression (no mention of lunging to bite or fighting) — this reads as a fear/frustration/over-arousal reactivity case, which is the most treatable kind.
- Because this is a rescue with unknown history, and reactivity training is easy to get subtly wrong (getting too close too fast, letting the dog "practice" the barking, or using leash corrections that add fear instead of removing it), a handful of paid coaching sessions in weeks 1-2 are worth the money to get your distance-management and reward-timing right. From week 3 on, you can run the plan yourself.
- Skip full board-and-train or a behaviorist — that level of intervention is for aggression/bite cases, not this.

## 2. If hiring — three South Bay options with real prices

| Trainer | Format & Price | Method | Area | Contact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **D For Dogz** (Kaajal Tiwary, CPDT-KA/KPA-CTP) | Leash Reactive Dog "Private Coaching": **$2,400 / 6 weeks** — 90-min initial consult + weekly 1:1 coaching in your home/neighborhood, priority text/call between sessions. (Trainer-led "Day Training" tier is $4,200/6 weeks — not needed here.) | Positive reinforcement only | San Jose, Sunnyvale, Santa Clara, Los Gatos, Mountain View, Campbell, Saratoga, Cupertino | (650) 538-3011 — free 15-min phone consult before you commit |
| **Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose** | "Aggressive/Reactive Dog Training": 8 lessons for **$1,200** (incl. e-collar + 20-ft leash). Cheaper entry: "Obedience Starter" — **$500 first lesson**, then **$100/session** after that, buy as many as needed. | E-collar / balanced (correction-based) | San Jose | (415) 200-4566 |
| **Lori Hamilton Dog Training** | Point-based Private Lesson package: **$1,500 for 10 points** — 1 point = facility/park session, 2 points = field-trip (pet store, downtown, dog playdate) or in-home session, spend flexibly. Program explicitly covers leash reactivity. | Mix of reward + correction | Los Gatos (14910 Los Gatos Blvd, Los Gatos, CA 95032) | (408) 320-5248 |

**General market context:** most South Bay trainers charge roughly $125-$210 per in-home visit for basic work, with reactivity/behavior cases priced at the higher end or sold as the multi-week packages above.

**If budget allows, start with D For Dogz** — it's the only one of the three that's purely positive-reinforcement (a better match for a rescue dog with unknown history), and the free 15-minute call costs you nothing to try. Get the other two as comparison quotes if price or scheduling doesn't line up.

## 3. Week-by-week plan (first 4 weeks)

Built around evenings (10-15 min/day) + weekends (30-45 min). Two tracks run every week: **(A)** loose-leash walking mechanics, **(B)** dog-reactivity desensitization.

**Gear first:** a front-clip no-pull harness (Easy Walk or Freedom harness — not a retractable leash, not a head halti unless a trainer fits it), a standard 6-ft leash, a treat pouch, and pea-sized high-value soft treats (cheese, chicken).

### Week 1 — Foundation & find the threshold
- **(A)** Daily evening backyard/quiet-street sessions: name response, "look at me," a few steps of loose-leash walking rewarded for staying at your side. Zero dog exposure yet.
- **(B)** One weekend outing with the sole goal of finding his **threshold distance** — how far away another dog can be before he notices but stays calm (no barking/fixating). Don't try to close that distance yet; just find it and log it (may be 50+ feet, may be across a parking lot).

### Week 2 — Pair calm with dogs at a distance
- **(A)** Continue daily LLW drills, now adding light distractions (a person walking by, a car).
- **(B)** On weekend walks, whenever another dog appears at or beyond threshold distance, mark and reward calm looking — the "Look At That" game (dog glances at trigger, you say "yes"/click, treat). If he tenses or fixates, you're too close — add distance immediately rather than push through it. Never let him rehearse the barking.

### Week 3 — Shrink the distance gradually
- **(A)** Move LLW practice into a quiet park path with mild distractions.
- **(B)** Same LAT game, a few feet closer each session — only advance once the current distance is reliably calm across multiple encounters. This is the slow part; don't rush it.

### Week 4 — Generalize
- **(A)** Practice loose-leash in busier real-world spots (busier trail, deeper into the neighborhood).
- **(B)** Same distance work in busier spots. **Checkpoint:** if he can pass most dogs at a reasonable distance without barking, keep extending the plan yourself into weeks 5+. If progress has stalled or he's still reacting most encounters, that's the signal to bring in the trainer from Section 2 rather than keep troubleshooting alone.

## Next steps for you
- Decide whether to call D For Dogz for the free 15-min consult (do this before week 1 if you want a coach in place from the start; otherwise it's fine to start the DIY plan solo and call in week 3/4 if reactivity work stalls).
- Buy the front-clip harness, 6-ft leash, and treats before week 1.
- Run the plan; if by end of week 4 there's been no real change in the barking, treat that as your trigger to book a trainer rather than continuing solo.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog-reactive barking
subtasks.description:
DECISION: Hybrid approach — do it yourself, but budget for 2-3 paid sessions with a professional trainer as a coaching layer, not full outsourcing.

Reasoning:
- Pulling on leash is a pure mechanical/reward-timing problem. Highly DIY-able with a standard loose-leash protocol (no professional needed for this part alone).
- Barking at every other dog is leash reactivity, which is very common in the breed and typically emotional (fear/frustration/over-arousal), not aggression. Research on border collies specifically confirms this pattern is normal for the breed's high visual/herding drive and is treatable with desensitization and counter-conditioning done at a safe distance, increasing exposure gradually.
- Because this is a rescue with an unknown history and the dog is still adolescent (14mo), and because reactivity training is easy to accidentally do wrong (e.g., letting the dog rehearse the behavior by getting too close too fast, or using leash corrections that increase fear), a few paid sessions with a trainer who specializes in reactivity are worth the money to get your distance-management and marker-timing right in weeks 1-2. After that, week 3-4 can be owner-run using the plan in subtask 'Draft week-by-week training plan'.
- No signs of aggression (no biting/fighting mentioned) so a full behaviorist or board-and-train program is not necessary — targeted private sessions are enough.

Bottom line: DIY the mechanics, hire a trainer for a short burst of coaching on the reactivity piece specifically.

subtasks.title: Draft week-by-week training plan for first 4 weeks
subtasks.description:
4-week owner-led plan, built around evening (10-15 min) and weekend (30-45 min) availability. Two tracks run in parallel every week: (A) loose-leash walking mechanics, (B) dog-reactivity desensitization/counter-conditioning. Full plan text is in the attached report on the parent task.

Gear to buy before week 1: front-clip harness (e.g. Easy Walk or Freedom No-Pull harness — NOT a retractable leash, NOT a head halti unless a trainer fits it), a sturdy 6-ft leash, a treat pouch, and pea-sized soft high-value treats (cheese, chicken, squeeze cheese).

Week 1 — Foundation & find the threshold: backyard/quiet-street engagement games (name response, "look at me"), loose-leash practice with zero dog exposure, and one weekend outing purely to find the dog's "threshold distance" from other dogs (the distance at which he notices but stays under threshold/doesn't bark) — do not close that distance yet.

Week 2 — Pair calm with dogs at a distance: continue LLW drills; on walks, whenever another dog appears at/beyond threshold distance, mark and reward calm looking (the "Look At That" game); if he starts to fixate or tense up, increase distance immediately rather than pushing through.

Week 3 — Shrink the distance gradually: same LAT game but a few feet closer each session, only advancing when the prior distance is reliably calm; keep LLW sessions going in busier low-key areas (quiet park paths).

Week 4 — Generalize: practice in busier real-world spots (busier trail, further into neighborhood) at whatever distance is currently calm; reassess — if he can pass most dogs at a reasonable distance without barking, keep extending; if progress has stalled or he's still barking most encounters, that's the signal to bring in a trainer (see other subtask) rather than keep DIY-ing past week 4.
